about: PIX-320, the Pixelheim Post's first step (Something to Come Back To, direction A): once Maren's first letter reaches Saltmere (`opens`, a main quest step's kind of condition), word goes round that Pixelheim has a courier who delivers anything, and a post box goes up on the square (`box`, beside the bounty board; `opened` is the line the log says as it does). Each game morning (DayNight's day, the one a night's sleep ends) the box holds up to `bag` pieces, worked out from the day, `seed` and the threads (Post.in_box): each thread offers its next piece once the one before it is delivered, a piece for someone where the hero has been, never past a shut gate (Gates), its sender home and its `when` met (a main quest step's kinds of condition, all of them). E at the box takes them into the satchel; walking up to a piece's addressee and pressing E hands it over: they say `said`, the courier is paid `tip` (and `gift`, an item, now and then), and a `reply` that follows it comes straight back into the satchel to carry home. A delivered piece's `words` read in the journal's Post tab, as Maren's letters do; `note` is what its outside says while it's sealed. `correspondents` are the people who write and are written to: the villager it's handed to (`npc`), and for one with no door of their own (Fafnyr, on Hilda's chimney) the villager who takes it for them. Nothing expires: a piece waits in the box or the satchel as long as it likes, and a day skipped costs nothing. Only what the hero did is saved (Post's own section of the save: the satchel, each thread's step, the pieces delivered and the day the box was last emptied).
opened: Word has reached Pixelheim: its courier delivers anything, even fifty years late. A post box goes up on the square, beside the bounty board.

pieces.note: A wheel of cheese in a sack. The label is in Bram's hand.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number one. Handle with care. Or don't. It's cheese.
said: Cheese? For me? Nobody sends me anything but weather.
(She sniffs it.) Tell Bram the gulls say thank you. No, wait. I'll write to him myself.

pieces.note: From Ola, in Saltmere. It smells of the harbour.
words: Dear Bram. Best cheese in Saltmere. Only cheese in Saltmere. The gulls got the rind. Send another, and a lid. - Ola
said: A lid! Why didn't I think of a lid?
The club has its first member, courier. Two, with me. Three, if you count the gulls.

pieces.note: A wheel of cheese, with a lid on it this time.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number two. Members get a wheel a week. Membership is free. You're a member now. No refunds.
said: We didn't join anything. ...Is that smoked?
Lads! Down tools! Cheese!

pieces.note: A hard old wheel. Bram has drawn a sword on the label, badly.
words: Bram's Cheese Club, wheel number three. For soldiers. Hard cheese for hard times. Don't throw it at anyone. Unless you must.
said: "Unless you must." Your Bram knows soldiers.
The lads will want to thank him properly. Hold on, courier. Somebody find a pen that isn't a spear.

pieces.note: Signed by Mabel and eleven soldiers. Two of them signed with a cross.
words: Dear Mister Bram. The garrison thanks the Cheese Club. Nobody threw it at anyone. The lads want to know: does the club have a song? - Mabel, and the lads
said: A song. The club needs a song.
Give me a week. Give me two. Here, courier, for your trouble: a wheel of your own. You're a member.

pieces.note: From Sela, at the inn. It smells of onions.
words: Mistress Wenna. A question from the inn's kitchen: how much salt goes in Tam's stew? I'd like to get it right before you taste it. - Sela
said: How much salt? Tell her: until the spoon stands up on its own.
Tam salted it like the sea. That's how you know it's from Saltmere.

pieces.note: From Wenna. Tam's sister's hand, firm and round.
words: To Old Pell, who had the canary. Maren's courier says you're still alive, and so is the bird. Tam wrote me once that she bit Morvax. Is it true? - Wenna, Tam's sister
said: (He reads it twice.) Tam's sister. Tam's sister!
Wait there, courier. This wants an answer, and the canary wants a say.

pieces.note: From Pell. Smudged with coal, with a small peck through one corner.
words: Mistress Wenna. She bit Morvax twice, and Maren once, by mistake. That was this one's great-great-grandmother. This one bites too. It runs in the family. - Pell
said: "It runs in the family." Ha! So does salt, in mine.

pieces.note: From the inn, next door. Written in a hurry.
words: Mister Pell. Your canary sang all night under my window. Every song she knows, twice. - W.
said: That's her welcome song. She likes Wenna.
Gods help her. Hold on, courier. The canary has something to add.

pieces.note: From Pell, over the forge. A yellow feather is tucked in the fold.
words: Mistress Wenna. The canary finds your stew too salty. The canary has never been wrong. - P.
said: Too salty. TOO SALTY.
Tam salted it like that for forty years and nobody died. Well. Not of the stew.

pieces.note: From Wenna. Folded twice, very neatly.
words: Mister Pell. A pot with no salt in it at all, tonight at six. Bring the bird. She can say it to my face. - W.
said: Supper. With Tam's sister.
...I'll wear the good coat. The canary will wear what she always wears: an opinion.

pieces.note: From Pip. There's a fish drawn on the envelope. Or a boot.
words: Dear Old Wenna. You come from the sea, so you know about fish. Does a dragon like fish? I am asking for a friend. The friend is a dragon. From Pip.
said: A dragon. Of course it is.
Well, a question deserves an answer. Take this back to the child.

pieces.note: From Old Wenna. It smells of the sea, and a little of stew.
words: Hello, Pip. Everything likes fish, except other fish. Ask your cat. - Old Wenna
said: "Ask your cat." I did. The cat said yes.
The cat says yes to everybody's fish. That's not science.

pieces.addressed: Letter for Mister Dragon, care of Hilda's chimney
pieces.note: From Pip. Addressed in very large letters, so a dragon can read it.
words: Dear Mister Dragon. Do you like fish? The cat says no. Write back. From Pip (not the cat).
said: A letter for the big lump on my chimney? I'll read it to him with his cheese.
(Hilda climbs the ladder. A long rumble on the roof. She comes down with a letter, scorched round the edges.) He moves his lips when he writes.

pieces.addressed: Reply for Pip, from the dragon
pieces.note: Scorched round the edges. Still warm.
words: Small human. Fish: acceptable. Cat: suspicious. Do not send the cat. - F.
said: He wrote back! It's all burnt at the edges!
"Do not send the cat." ...I wasn't going to send the cat. Was I going to send the cat?

pieces.addressed: Letter for Mister Dragon, care of Hilda's chimney
pieces.note: From Pip. There are paw prints on it.
words: Dear Mister Dragon. I did not send the cat. The cat went by itself. Sorry. From Pip.
said: So that's what's been on my chimney all morning.
(Another rumble on the roof, a long one. A letter flutters down, smoking a little.)

pieces.addressed: Reply for Pip, from the dragon
pieces.note: Scorched round the edges. A cat's hair is stuck in the wax.
words: Small human. The cat sleeps on my tail. It is warm. I have decided to allow it. Do not tell the cat. - F.
said: I won't tell. ...The cat knows.
